product.title: Turkish 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Turkish: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that take every word apart ending by ending, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Turkish is friendlier than its reputation: no gender, no articles, almost no irregular verbs, and a spelling that is read exactly as written. Each unit tackles one of the three things that really are different for English speakers: vowel harmony, six cases attached to the end of the noun, and a verb that always comes last in the sentence.

blocks.text: Open a Turkish dictionary to almost any page and sooner or later you will stop, because a word looks familiar. *Otobüs* is a bus. *Tren* is a train. *Bilet* is a ticket, *asansör* an elevator, *kuaför* a hairdresser, *müze* a museum. Turkish took hundreds of words from French and Italian and simply respelled them the way they sound — and it gave a few back: *yogurt*, *kebab*, *kiosk* and *coffee* all reached English through Turkish.

Even more words came from Arabic and Persian over centuries of Ottoman history: *kitap* (book), *kalem* (pen), *dünya* (world), *insan* (human being), *misafir* (guest). If you know any Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Hindi, Malay or Indonesian, many of them will feel like old friends. Either way, you start this language with a few hundred words for free, and that is real capital.

But the resemblance stops exactly where it matters most: **how sentences are built**. English builds meaning from separate words lined up in a row — *in my house*, *can't come*. Turkish builds it by **sticking pieces onto the end of a single word**, one after another, until the word itself becomes a sentence. *Ev* is house. *Evim* is my house. *Evimde* is in my house. *Evimdeyim* is I'm in my house. Five English words, one Turkish word.

That is why this course never asks you to memorize long words whole. From the first unit, every line of dialogue is taken apart in its literal line: *ev-im-de-yim* → "house-my-in-I-am". Once you are used to seeing the joins, no word is too long to face — it is just a stack of pieces that always come in the same order.

One law governs that whole stack, and it is set up in Unit 2, not tucked away in an appendix: **vowel harmony**. Turkish endings have no single fixed form; they adapt to the last vowel of the word they attach to. So "in" can be *-de*, *-da*, *-te* or *-ta*, and all four are the same ending. Learners who master this law in their first week learn the rest of the language calmly; those who put it off end up memorizing thousands of forms that are really one.

The third thing to know from the start: **the verb almost always comes at the end of the sentence**, and a Turkish sentence holds back its key information until the last moment. *Ben yarın Ankara'ya gideceğim* — "I tomorrow to-Ankara will-go". An English ear wants to know right away what is happening; a Turkish ear waits patiently. That patience can be trained, and the short dialogues in this course are the training.

The good news is that, beyond those three things, Turkish is far friendlier than its reputation. There is no grammatical gender. There is no article like *the*. There are hardly any irregular verbs — the language has essentially one, *demek* (to say), and very few other exceptions. The spelling is read exactly as it is written: once you know the sounds of its 29 letters, you can read signs, menus and tickets correctly without ever guessing.

The twenty units ahead follow one storyline: Budi, a student from Indonesia, lands in Istanbul, looks for a room, learns to shop at the market, orders food, gets lost, falls ill, is invited to a Turkish family's home, and finally tells the story of his vacation in Cappadocia. The characters and places keep coming back from unit to unit, so old vocabulary keeps working while new words are added.

After Unit 20 you won't be fluent. But you will be able to walk into a shop in Kadıköy, ask the price, haggle a little, explain where you come from, and understand the answer. That is no small thing. *Kolay gelsin* — may it come easy to you.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses the endings put in place by the units before it.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Turkish out loud without looking at the translation. Turkish spelling is read exactly as written, so you can get it right from day one.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most often, yet it is where every ending is taken apart, one by one. Example: *Türkçeyi seviyorum* is written "Turkish-the am-loving-I", and *arkadaşımlayım* becomes "friend-my-with-I-am".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with its pronunciation. The stressed syllable is written in CAPITAL LETTERS.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Turkish, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Turkish sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit that decides everything
items: Every time you meet a new word, don't just learn its meaning — look at its **last vowel**. That vowel decides the shape of every ending that will later attach to it.
*Ev* ends in *e* → *evde*. *Okul* ends in *u* → *okulda*. This tiny habit saves months of confusion.

blocks.title: Turkey or Türkiye?
items: Since 2022 the country's official name in English has been *Türkiye*, though *Turkey* is still widely used. The language is **Turkish** in English; in Turkish itself the country is *Türkiye* and the language is *Türkçe*.
This course writes *Türkiye* inside Turkish sentences and "Turkey" in the English text.

blocks.text: Before Unit 1, collect what's free. The words below are already in your head — you just didn't know Turks use them too. Most came into Turkish from French and Italian and were respelled the way they sound; a few traveled the other way, from Turkish into English.
Almost the same sound, the same meaning
Looks familiar, means something else — careful
Borrowed from Arabic and Persian

A second, older layer came from Arabic and Persian during the Ottoman centuries. If you know any of those languages — or Urdu, Hindi, Malay or Indonesian, which drew from the same source — hundreds of everyday words will open up on their own: *kitap* (book), *kalem* (pen), *insan* (human being), *hayvan* (animal), *dünya* (world), *akıl* (mind), *sebep* (reason), *vakit* (time), *hediye* (gift), *misafir* (guest), *selam* (greeting), *cevap* (answer), *haber* (news), *hayat* (life), *lezzet* (flavor). And *bilgisayar* (computer)? That one is pure Turkish: "knowledge counter".

blocks.title: How many, really?
items: A large modern Turkish dictionary lists around six thousand words of Arabic origin, over a thousand from Persian, and several thousand from French. Not all of them are everyday words — but the ones you meet on signs, menus and tickets very often are.
In other words: even from zero, you are not really starting from zero. What you need to build is the frame — endings and word order — and that is what these twenty units are for.

blocks.text: Turkish has used the Latin alphabet since 1928, and its spelling was designed as **one letter, one sound**. There are no silent letters and no letter pairs that make a different sound (no *th*, no *gh*). Once you know the list below, you can read anything correctly — including words you have never seen.

The "Say it" column in this course keeps the Turkish vowels with fixed values: **a** as in "father", **e** as in "bed" (never silent, never "ee"), **i** as in "machine" but short, **o** as in "more", **u** as in "put" or "moon". A few spellings are changed to help English readers: **ch** for *ç*, **sh** for *ş*, **zh** for *j*, **uh** for *ı*, and **ai** (as in *chai*) for a syllable-final *ay*. *Ö* and *ü* stay as they are. A doubled vowel (**aa**, **öö**) is a long vowel.

blocks.title: ı and i are two different letters
items: This is beginners' mistake number one. *ı* (no dot) and *i* (with a dot) are not style variants — they are different letters, like *a* and *e*. Their capitals differ too: *ı* → **I**, while *i* → **İ** (a capital with a dot).
That is why the city is written **İstanbul**, not *Istanbul*. And *açık* (open) is said "a-CHUHK" with that unrounded *uh* sound, not "a-cheek".
Mixing them up is not just a matter of accent: *sık* (often) and *sik* are two very different words, and the second one is vulgar. Watch the dot.

blocks.text: The letter ğ — a letter that works silently

*Yumuşak g* ("soft g") never starts a word and is never pronounced as a *g*. Its job is to lengthen the vowel in front of it: *dağ* (mountain) is said "daa", *ağaç* (tree) "a-ACH", *öğretmen* (teacher) "öö-ret-MEN". Between two front vowels it melts into a light *y*: *değil* (not) sounds like "de-YIL".
Word stress

The default rule is simple: **stress falls on the last syllable**, and it moves along every time a new ending is attached. *Ev* → *ev-DE* → *ev-de-YIM*. That is why Turkish words seem to rise toward the end.

There are three groups of exceptions to recognize now, because they all come up often: place names are often stressed in the middle or at the front (*İS-tan-bul*, *AN-ka-ra*, *AN-tal-ya*); question words are stressed at the front (*NE-re-de*, *NA-suhl*); and the negative ending *-me/-ma* pulls the stress onto the syllable **before** it (*GEL-mi-yo-rum*, I'm not coming).

blocks.title: The ^ mark over a vowel
items: Now and then you'll see *â*, *î* or *û*: *kâğıt* (paper), *hâlâ* (still), *rüzgâr* (wind). The mark softens the *k*/*g*/*l* before it and sometimes lengthens the vowel.
There are only a few such words, and the mark is often left out in everyday writing. Don't let it weigh on you — just don't be surprised when you see it.

blocks.text: Vowel harmony — the law that governs everything
2-form endings: plural *-ler/-lar*, location *-de/-da*, direction *-e/-a*, origin *-den/-dan*. 4-form endings: object *-i*, possessive *-im*, question *mi*, and *-lı*, *-ci*.
Consonant harmony

items: After the hard consonants **f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p** (memorized as *FiSTiKÇi ŞaHaP*), a *d* at the start of an ending becomes *t*: *iş-te*, *kitap-tan*, *genç-tir*.
The consonants **p, ç, t, k** at the end of a word soften to **b, c, d, ğ** when an ending starting with a vowel is attached: *kitap → kitabım*, *ağaç → ağacı*, *dört → dördü*, *sokak → sokağa*.
When two vowels meet, a buffer letter is inserted: **y** for direction/object (*Ankara-y-a*), **n** after a possessive ending (*evi-n-de*), **s** for third-person possessive (*araba-s-ı*).

Negating and asking

items: **Verbs** are negated with *-me/-ma* before the tense ending: *gel-mi-yorum* (I'm not coming), *gel-me-dim* (I didn't come), *gel-me-yeceğim* (I won't come).
**Nouns / adjectives** are negated with the separate word *değil*: *öğrenci değilim* (I'm not a student), *pahalı değil* (it's not expensive).
**Existence** is negated with *yok*, not *değil*: *param yok* (I have no money).
**Yes/no questions** use *mı/mi/mu/mü*, written SEPARATELY and placed after the word being asked about: *Geliyor musun?*, *Öğrenci misin?*, *Var mı?*

blocks.text: Ten of the most common linking words
The dictionary form of a Turkish verb always ends in *-mek* or *-mak*, and vowel harmony decides which. Drop that ending and what's left is the root — the place every other ending attaches to.

blocks.title: Compound verbs with etmek
items: Many borrowed words become verbs by adding *etmek* (to do) or *olmak* (to become): *telefon etmek* (to phone), *kabul etmek* (to accept), *dans etmek* (to dance), *yardım etmek* (to help), *memnun olmak* (to be pleased), *hasta olmak* (to fall ill).
Only *etmek*/*olmak* changes; the word in front stays put: *yardım ediyorum*, *yardım ettim*, *yardım edeceğim*.

blocks.title: The only irregular verbs
items: *Demek* (to say) and *yemek* (to eat) shorten their vowel in some forms: *diyorum* (I say, not *deyorum*), *yiyorum* (I'm eating, not *yeyorum*).
*Gitmek* (to go) and *etmek* soften *t* to *d* before a vowel: *gidiyorum*, *ediyorum*. Beyond these, there is no list of irregular verbs to memorize — everything else follows the rules.

blocks.text: If you've reached this page after genuinely working through all twenty units, your level is roughly **full A1, heading toward A2**: you can introduce yourself, shop, order food, ask for directions, talk about yesterday, and share your plans. What you don't have yet is speed — and no book can give you that.
Three things that raise your level fastest

items: **Watch Turkish TV series with Turkish subtitles**, not English ones. *Diziler* are full of short, repeated sentences and everyday language that never makes it into textbooks. Start by watching the same episode three times.
**Read menus, signs and tickets.** They all follow the same patterns as Units 9 and 10, and every new word proves its use right away. Istanbul's transit apps in Turkish are a free workbook.
**Talk to people.** Turks almost always praise a foreigner who tries, and almost never switch to English if you hold out in Turkish for two or three more sentences.

blocks.text: What's waiting for you at A2

items: **Relative clauses with *-diği*** — Turkish's way of saying "that", "which", "when" and "what": *geldiğim gün* (the day I came), *ne dediğini anlamadım* (I didn't understand what he said). This is the door to long sentences.
**The full *-miş* form** — the way to mark news you didn't witness yourself. In Unit 20 you only meet it; at A2 it becomes a storytelling tool.

**Passive, reciprocal and causative verbs** (*-il*, *-iş*, *-dir*): *açılmak* (to be opened), *görüşmek* (to meet each other), *yaptırmak* (to have something made). Turkish builds new verbs from roots you already have.

blocks.text: And if you'd like a human by your side, not just pages — Linguo's Turkish classes run every week, from A1 to B2, with teachers who know where learners get stuck. *Kolay gelsin, görüşürüz!*
